title: T1021.002 — Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.

steps.title: Stolen hash, no password needed
steps.caption: A phishing email gave the attacker control of INT-WS-07. They dump the memory of lsass.exe and get the NTLM hash of a domain admin. A hash is a password fingerprint: Windows accepts it for many remote logons, so the real password is never needed.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: List what the server shares
steps.caption: First the attacker looks around. A connection to IPC$, the communication channel share, lets them ask FS01 which shares it offers. The hidden ones show up: ADMIN$, C$, IPC$, and a data share called Finance$. To the server this looks like a plain network logon.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Open the hidden ADMIN$ share
steps.caption: Using only the stolen hash, the attacker maps ADMIN$ - the share that points into the Windows folder of FS01. The server records a Type 3 network logon and the file check inside the share. No failed logons appear, because the hash simply works.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Drop the tool into ADMIN$
steps.caption: The attacker copies their payload, tool.dll, into the Temp folder inside ADMIN$. The file physically lands on FS01, so the write is logged there by Sysmon, not on the attacker's machine. Staging a file first is the standard pattern before remote execution.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Run it as SYSTEM with a fake service
steps.caption: Now the payload runs. The attacker asks the Service Control Manager on FS01 to create a service called PGMsgSvc that launches the dropped DLL, then starts it. Services run as SYSTEM, the strongest local account. The service install is the loudest event so far.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Same trick on the domain controller
steps.caption: The same hash opens ADMIN$ on DC01, the domain controller. A second service launches the payload there. Reaching a domain controller means the attacker can now create accounts, read every password hash in the domain, and do anything else they want.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Read HR files through C$
steps.caption: With admin rights everywhere, the attacker maps C$ on the workstation HR-PC05 and reads files from a user's Documents folder. No service is created and nothing is changed - only 5145 records show which files were opened. Quiet reads like this are easy to miss.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: How defenders catch this
steps.caption: In the SIEM, the pieces connect. One rule flags executable writes into ADMIN$; another chains the Type 3 logon with the share access from the same source. The 7045 installs and the services.exe process chain confirm it. The hunted host was a workstation - admins should work from jump servers.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.
